For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s a common dilemma—on one hand a registry can make the whole gift‑giving process smoother for everyone; on the other hand, some people (and especially parents) feel that it’s a bit “pushy” to tell guests exactly what to buy. The good news is that you can keep the benefits of a registry while still honoring your mother’s feelings. Here are a few ways to strike that balance: --- ## 1. Keep the Registry, but Make It *Optional* - **Share the registry link only with close friends and family** who you know will appreciate the convenience. - In your invitation or wedding website, add a short note: > “We’re excited to celebrate with you! If you’d like to give a gift, we’ve set up a registry. If you prefer to give something else (cash, experience, or a handmade item), that’s perfectly fine too.” This signals that the registry is a helpful tool, not a requirement. --- ## 2. Offer a “Wish List” Instead of a Full Registry - A wish list can be a simple Google Sheet or a private list on a site like Etsy. - You can include a mix of items you truly need and a few “nice‑to‑have” pieces. - Label it as a *wish list* rather than a *registry* to soften the tone. --- ## 3. Combine a Registry with a “Gift Card” Option - Many couples add a small gift‑card section (e.g., $50‑$100) to the registry. - This gives guests the freedom to choose something they love while still giving you something useful. - You can phrase it as: > “If you’d rather give a gift card, we’ve added a few options to the registry.” --- ## 4. Communicate with Your Mother - **Explain the practical side**: “We’re trying to avoid duplicate gifts and make sure we have the essentials for our new life together.” - **Reassure her**: “We’re not forcing anyone to buy something from the list. It’s just a convenience for those who want to.” - **Invite her input**: “If you have any items you think would be perfect, we’d love to add them to the list.” Sometimes a short conversation can turn a concern into a collaborative effort. --- ## 5. Keep the Registry Private (If You’re Really Concerned) - Some registries allow you to keep the list hidden until after the wedding. - You can still use the registry to order items you need, but you won’t share the link with guests. - This way, you get the benefits without any “public” pressure. --- ## 6. Use a “Thank‑You” Note to Clarify - After the wedding, send a thank‑you card that says: > “Thank you for celebrating with us! We’re grateful for your presence and any gift you chose to give. If you used the registry, we appreciate your help in getting us ready for our new life.” This acknowledges the registry while also showing that you value the gesture, not the item. --- ## Bottom Line - **Yes, you can still use a registry**—just make it clear that it’s optional and that you appreciate any gift, not just those from the list. - **Frame it as a convenience** rather than a directive. - **Communicate openly** with your mother (and other family members) so they feel respected and included. By blending practicality with sensitivity, you’ll keep the registry’s benefits while honoring your mother’s perspective. Good luck with your wedding planning!
